title: Student Engagement with GenAI’s Tutoring Feedback: A Mixed Methods Study
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students engage with immediate AI-generated tutoring feedback in introductory programming education. The authors argue that feedback effectiveness depends not only on feedback quality, but also on students’ engagement with that feedback—specifically how they perceive, interpret, and use it. The study addresses two questions: what students think while interacting with different tutoring feedback components, and how those thoughts relate to visual attention and immediate problem-solving actions.

To investigate this, the authors built a Python programming learning environment, Tutor Kai, that provides four types of GenAI tutoring feedback: Find Problems, Explanations and Examples, Next Step Hint, and Strategic Approach. Feedback was generated with OpenAI’s gpt-4.1 model and presented as individually selectable components. The study used a mixed-methods design combining think-aloud protocols, eye-tracking, screen recordings, logs, and a questionnaire. The analysis focused on which feedback components students requested and read, what they verbalized while processing them, and whether they subsequently improved their code, made no change, or took a counterproductive step.

The participants were 20 undergraduate students enrolled in an introductory programming course at a German university, primarily in their first or second semester. Data collection took place during the third and fourth weeks of the summer semester of 2025. Students completed programming tasks in a supervised lab setting using standard computing equipment and Tobii eye-tracking glasses. Across 172 GenAI feedback requests, 688 feedback components were generated; students selectively opened 384 of them, and almost all opened components were read.

The main findings are that students most often verbalized understanding, but also frequently expressed a need for additional information or disagreement with the feedback. When students expressed understanding, the related feedback often led to code improvements. When they expressed disagreement or needed more information, they typically did not act immediately on the feedback and instead opened another feedback component. Overall, the study concludes that students actively self-regulate their use of AI tutoring feedback rather than passively accepting it, and that students’ internal evaluation of feedback is a key factor in whether AI-generated tutoring feedback supports learning. The authors suggest that future systems should better support follow-up questioning and feedback literacy.

identified_tools.name: Tutor Kai
identified_tools.description: A programming learning environment for Python exercises that provides immediate AI-generated tutoring feedback through four components: Find Problems, Explanations and Examples, Next Step Hint, and Strategic Approach.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an online environment for introductory programming students solving Python tasks, where students could request and selectively open AI-generated tutoring feedback components while researchers analyzed attention, think-aloud responses, and immediate code actions.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods study of 20 undergraduate students, 172 GenAI feedback requests were made in Tutor Kai, generating 688 feedback components; students collected 384 (55.8%) and read 380 of those. Overall, in 141 of 172 feedback requests (82.0%), at least one collected/read component resulted in an improvement to student code.
findings.measure: Immediate code improvement following AI-generated tutoring feedback during Python problem solving
findings.effect_size: 82.0% of feedback requests resulted in at least one improvement

findings.finding_summary: Students acted upon 201 of 380 read feedback components (52.9%), resulting in improvement (160 cases), setback (13 cases), or both improvement and setback (28 cases). The Next Step Hint component most frequently led to improvement, doing so in 38 of 73 read instances (52.1%), compared with 69 of 166 for Find Problems, 42 of 111 for Explanations and Examples, and 11 of 30 for Strategic Approach.
findings.measure: Immediate code actions after reading feedback components, including improvement/setback rates by component

findings.finding_summary: When students’ verbalized thoughts indicated understanding, 76.2% of related feedback components led to code improvements. Conversely, when students expressed disagreement or a need for additional information, 69.5% of related feedback components led to no immediate code action, and in 79.2% of those no-action cases students instead collected another feedback component.
findings.measure: Relation between think-aloud engagement categories and immediate code actions
findings.effect_size: 76.2% improvement after understanding; 69.5% no action after disagreement/additional-info needs; 79.2% collected another component in no-action cases
findings.sample_size: n=20; based on coded read feedback components

findings.finding_summary: Analysis of 314 coded think-aloud instances tied to 380 read feedback components found four themes in student engagement: expressions of understanding (45.5%), additional information needed (21.6%), disagreement (18.7%), and explicit judgments of helpfulness (14.3%). These results indicate students actively evaluated feedback rather than uniformly accepting it, with selective uptake depending on perceived relevance and clarity.
findings.measure: Think-aloud coded categories reflecting feedback engagement, interpretation, and self-regulated response
findings.effect_size: 45.5% understanding; 21.6% additional information needed; 18.7% disagreement; 14.3% explicit judgments

findings.finding_summary: Students selectively used Tutor Kai’s feedback rather than opening everything available: they collected 384 of 688 generated components (55.8%), and almost all collected components were read (380 of 384, about 99%). Collection frequency decreased in interface order from Find Problems to Explanations and Examples to Next Step Hint to Strategic Approach, suggesting students self-directed their information seeking.
findings.measure: Feedback uptake and reading behavior within the tutoring interface

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with eye-tracking, think-aloud protocols, logs, and questionnaire data, but it is qualitative/exploratory and does not use an RCT or quasi-experimental design. The sample is small (n=20 analyzed), so causal claims about learning effectiveness are limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising improvement rates in immediate coding actions, but effects are descriptive percentages rather than standardized learning gains, and no effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported. Impact on broader academic outcomes is therefore positive but still unclear in magnitude.
